title: Data Structures: Stacks and Queues Quiz

stem.text:
A program must store up to one million integers. Which comparison between an
array-based stack and a linked-list stack is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: An array-based stack must shift every element on each pop

options.label: B
options.text: A linked-list stack cannot support O(1) push and pop

options.label: C
options.text: A linked-list stack always uses less memory because it has no unused capacity

options.label: D
options.text: An array-based stack may reserve unused capacity, while a linked-list stack has per-node link and allocation overhead

stem.text:
A stack receives distinct integers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 pushed in that order. You may pop at any
time between pushes. Each pop will represent the output sequence. Which output sequence is
impossible?

A circular queue of capacity 5 uses count to distinguish empty from full. front = rear =
2. What can be concluded from the two indices alone?

options.label: A
options.text: The queue is definitely empty

options.label: B
options.text: The queue could be empty or full; count must be checked

options.label: C
options.text: The queue contains exactly two elements

options.label: D
options.text: The queue is definitely full

stem.text:
A circular queue uses an array of length 6 and count. front = 4, rear = 1, and count = 3.
The stored values are array[4] = 10, array[5] = 20, and array[0] = 30. What happens after dequeue(),
then enqueue(40)?

options.label: A
options.text: Returns 10; front = 5, rear = 2, count = 3

options.label: B
options.text: Returns 20; front = 0, rear = 2, count = 3

options.label: C
options.text: Returns 30; front = 5, rear = 2, count = 3

options.label: D
options.text: Returns 10; front = 5, rear = 1, count = 2

stem.text:
An array-based stack uses top = -1 to represent an empty stack. The array has capacity
6. After push(10), push(20), pop(), push(30), what is top?

A stack is implemented using a singly linked list with only a head pointer. Which
design allows both push and pop to take O(1) time?

options.label: A
options.text: Push and pop at the head

options.label: B
options.text: Push and pop at the tail

options.label: C
options.text: Push at the head and pop at the tail

options.label: D
options.text: Push at the tail and pop at the head

stem.text:
A noncircular array queue increments rear on enqueue and front on dequeue without
shifting elements. rear reaches the end of the array, although earlier dequeues have freed slots at
the beginning. What is the underlying problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The implementation cannot reuse the freed slots without shifting or wrapping

options.label: B
options.text: The array has automatically reduced its capacity

options.label: C
options.text: The queue has violated FIFO ordering

options.label: D
options.text: The queue must actually contain as many elements as the array length

stem.text:
A circular queue uses an array of length 8 (indexed 0 to 7) and an integer variable
count to track the number of stored elements. front points to the next item to remove; rear points
to the next free slot. Initially assume that front and rear both are at index 6, that is, front = rear = 6
and count = 0. After five enqueues followed by two dequeues, what are front, rear, and the number
of items (count)?

options.label: A
options.text: front = 0, rear = 2, items = 2

options.label: B
options.text: front = 0, rear = 3, items = 3

options.label: C
options.text: front = 6, rear = 3, items = 5

options.label: D
options.text: front = 1, rear = 3, items = 2

stem.text:
A student grows an array-based stack by exactly one slot whenever it becomes full.
Starting with capacity 1, what is the total time for n pushes, including copying during resizing?

options.label: A
options.text: O(n)

options.label: B
options.text: O(n squared)

options.label: C
options.text: O(log n)

options.label: D
options.text: O(n log n)

stem.text:
A queue is implemented using two stacks named "IN" and "OUT". That is, queue
order (FIFO) will be obtained with the help of two stacks (which are LIFO). Enqueue: push data
onto stack IN. Dequeue: transfers all the elements from IN to OUT but only when OUT is empty,
otherwise nothing is transferred. Then pop out from OUT.
Now, starting empty, execute enqueue(10), enqueue(20), dequeue(), enqueue(30), enqueue(40),
dequeue(), dequeue(). What do the three dequeue operations return?

A student implements a stack using a singly linked list with head and tail pointers,
placing the stack top at the tail. Why does pop generally take O(n) time?

options.label: A
options.text: The value at the tail cannot be read directly

options.label: B
options.text: The entire list must be copied into a new list

options.label: C
options.text: The predecessor of the tail must be found by traversal

options.label: D
options.text: Every node must have its value shifted

stem.text:
A student implements a queue using a singly linked list with head and tail pointers.
Enqueue inserts at the head, and dequeue removes from the head. What behavior does this
implementation actually provide?

options.label: A
options.text: FIFO queue behavior

options.label: B
options.text: Priority queue behavior

options.label: C
options.text: Circular queue behavior

options.label: D
options.text: LIFO stack behavior

stem.text:
A stack implements getMin() using an auxiliary stack called MIN. When pushing a
value, it is also pushed onto MIN if MIN is empty or the value is less than or equal to MIN's top.
When popping a value, MIN is also popped if MIN's top equals that value.
Starting with both stacks empty, execute: push(8), push(4), push(6), push(2), push(2), pop(), pop().
What does getMin() return now, and why does it take O(1) time?

options.label: A
options.text: 4, because the top of MIN holds the current minimum and can be read directly.

options.label: B
options.text: 6, because the top of the main stack is always its minimum.

options.label: C
options.text: 2, because MIN permanently stores the smallest value ever pushed.

options.label: D
options.text: 4, because getMin() scans the main stack to find its smallest value.

stem.text:
A queue uses a singly linked list with front and rear pointers. Initially it is empty. After
enqueue(10), enqueue(20), dequeue(), dequeue(), and enqueue(30), which statement must be true
in a correct implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: front is null and rear points to the node containing 30

options.label: B
options.text: front points to the node containing 30 and rear is null

options.label: C
options.text: front points to the node containing 20 and rear points to the node containing 30

options.label: D
options.text: front and rear both point to the node containing 30

stem.text:
A FIFO queue uses a singly linked list with only a head pointer. It enqueues at the tail
and dequeues at the head. What are the time complexities?

options.label: A
options.text: Enqueue O(1), dequeue O(1)

options.label: B
options.text: Enqueue O(1), dequeue O(n)

options.label: C
options.text: Enqueue O(n), dequeue O(n)

options.label: D
options.text: Enqueue O(n), dequeue O(1)

stem.text:
An array-based stack of object references pops an element by decreasing top but
leaves the reference in the old array slot. What problem can this cause in a garbage-collected
language?

options.label: A
options.text: The popped object may remain reachable thereby delaying garbage collection

options.label: B
options.text: The stack immediately becomes a queue

options.label: C
options.text: The remaining elements change their order

options.label: D
options.text: The next push must take O(n) time

stem.text:
An array-based stack stores n elements and doubles its capacity whenever full. What
is the time complexity of a push that triggers resizing, and the time complexity of other push
operations?

options.label: A
options.text: O(log n) for resizing push and O(1) otherwise

options.label: B
options.text: O(n) for resizing push and O(1) otherwise

options.label: C
options.text: O(n) for both

options.label: D
options.text: O(1) for both

stem.text:
An initially empty queue Q receives A, B, C, D in that order (that is, A was enqueued
first and D was enqueued last). Execute: while Q is not empty, push( Q.dequeue() ) onto stack S;
then while S is not empty, enqueue S.pop() into Q. Finally execute: Q.enqueue(Q.dequeue()) twice.
What is Q from front to rear? (that is, read the answers from left to right)

options.label: A
options.text: A, B, C, D

options.label: B
options.text: C, D, A, B

options.label: C
options.text: B, A, D, C

options.label: D
options.text: D, C, B, A

stem.text:
A circular queue of length 8 contains five items in FIFO order at indices 6, 7, 0, 1, and
2. It is resized to length 16 by copying the items in FIFO order into indices 0 through 4. front points
to the next removal and rear to the next insertion. What should the new front and rear be?

options.label: A
options.text: front = 5, rear = 0

options.label: B
options.text: front = 6, rear = 3

options.label: C
options.text: front = 0, rear = 4

options.label: D
options.text: front = 0, rear = 5

stem.text:
A linked-list queue maintains front and rear pointers. It contains exactly one node.
After dequeue removes that node, which update is required?

options.label: A
options.text: Make the removed node point to itself

options.label: B
options.text: Set front to null and leave rear unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Set both front and rear to null

options.label: D
options.text: Set rear to null and leave front unchanged
